entries.title: Was Homer’s Ithaca Really an Island?: New Research Challenges a 2,000-Year-Old Assumption
entries.summary: Even if we didn’t make it to a screening of Christopher Nolan’s big-screen adaptation this past summer — and indeed, even if we’ve never read Homer’s original epic at all — we know that the Odyssey tells the story of a ten-year-long journey back to Ithaca. The narrative’s urgency doesn’t arise from the fact that its protagonist, the […]
entries.content:
Even if we did­n’t make it to a screen­ing of Christo­pher Nolan’s big-screen adap­ta­tion this past sum­mer — and indeed, even if we’ve nev­er read Home­r’s orig­i­nal epic at all — we know that the Odyssey tells the sto­ry of a ten-year-long jour­ney back to Itha­ca. The nar­ra­tive’s urgency does­n’t arise from the fact that its pro­tag­o­nist, the king Odysseus, has class­es at Cor­nell to teach. In fact, he may not even be try­ing to get back to the extant Greek island cel­e­brat­ed for bear­ing that same name. So, at least, argues a recent paper by two dis­tin­guished pro­fes­sors, Cam­bridge’s James Dig­gle and the Uni­ver­si­ty of Aberdeen’s John Under­hill. You can read “Was Home­r’s Itha­ca an Island?” at the online jour­nal Antigone.

Alter­na­tive­ly, you can watch the new video from clas­si­cist-nov­el­ist Hon­or Cargill-Mar­tin above. The real Greek island of Itha­ca, or Itha­ki, with its pic­turesque ham­lets and lime­stone mono­liths, “actu­al­ly does­n’t match, pret­ty much at all, the descrip­tion that Homer gives us of Itha­ca,” she says.

Hav­ing sailed there last sum­mer, she can describe it as “an amaz­ing place, so dra­mat­ic and so evoca­tive, but in large part, that’s because the moun­tains essen­tial­ly rise straight out of the sea” — a direct con­tra­dic­tion to Home­r’s lines about low­lands sur­round­ing a sin­gle cen­tral peak. Did he just get it wrong? Or was he tak­ing artis­tic license in order to imag­ine the kind of place from which a hero like Odysseus would come forth, despite the fact that he got his geog­ra­phy more or less right else­where?

In 2005, a man­age­ment con­sul­tant called Robert Bit­tle­stone put forth the argu­ment that Homer’s Itha­ca was actu­al­ly Pali­ki, a penin­su­la on the west­ern edge of Kefalo­nia. In order to test this the­o­ry, Bit­tle­stone brought in Dig­gle and Under­hill, his col­lab­o­ra­tors on the book Odysseus Unbound: The Search for Home­r’s Itha­ca. Now, a decade after Bit­tle­stone’s death, the oth­ers have pro­duced new geo­log­i­cal and tex­tu­al evi­dence for the Pali­ki hypoth­e­sis, not least that Homer nev­er once explic­it­ly calls Itha­ca an island, or even describes it in terms he applies to known islands. Cargill-Mar­tin finds their research “extreme­ly con­vinc­ing,” which makes you won­der: will Itha­ca take down its stat­ue of Odysseus in response? Prob­a­bly not, but at least we’ll have some­thing to talk about when we go stand before it.

via Boing Boing

entries.title: The Man Who Risked His Life Mocking the Nazis: Read 96 Issues of His Underground Magazine, Created in Hiding During WWII
entries.summary: The word zine, referring to a homemade magazine not distributed through the normal commercial channels, has a longer history than you might expect. Its earliest recorded uses date from 1946 in the world of pulp magazines, most often of the science-fiction variety. But just a year earlier, as it happens, one of the most historically […]
entries.content:
The word zine, refer­ring to a home­made mag­a­zine not dis­trib­uted through the nor­mal com­mer­cial chan­nels, has a longer his­to­ry than you might expect. Its ear­li­est record­ed uses date from 1946 in the world of pulp mag­a­zines, most often of the sci­ence-fic­tion vari­ety. But just a year ear­li­er, as it hap­pens, one of the most his­tor­i­cal­ly notable zines avant la let­tre con­clud­ed pub­li­ca­tion. The end of World War II had every­thing to do with it, since Het Onder­wa­ter-Cabaret, or The Under­wa­ter Cabaret, exist­ed as a rebuke against the Nazi occu­pa­tion of the Nether­lands. Over its two-year run, it put out 96 issues, total­ing over 1,700 pages full of art and poems — all cre­at­ed by one man in hid­ing in an attic.

Born to a Jew­ish fam­i­ly in Dort­mund in 1908, Curt Bloch stud­ied law with aspi­ra­tions of becom­ing a judge. When Hitler rose to pow­er, his plans changed: he first left for Ams­ter­dam, and lat­er, when Ger­many invad­ed the Nether­lands in 1940, he had to keep mov­ing until he end­ed up in the bor­der town of Enschede.

The resis­tance net­work Group Over­duin even­tu­al­ly placed him in the pri­vate home of an under­tak­er and a house­keep­er who had already tak­en in two oth­er Jews. Despite the lack of space and resources, he man­aged to pro­duce Het Onder­wa­ter-Cabaret using sup­plies deliv­ered along with the refugees’ food. Only one hand-assem­bled, thread-stitched copy of each issue exist­ed, to be cir­cu­lat­ed between some 20 to 30 sim­i­lar­ly hid­den read­ers before being returned to the attic.

By the end of the war, Bloch resur­faced to free­dom with every issue of Het Onder­wa­ter-Cabaret intact and in his pos­ses­sion. Bound into vol­umes in Ams­ter­dam, they accom­pa­nied him when he emi­grat­ed to the Unit­ed States, where he went on to raise a fam­i­ly. As the sto­ry is told in the His­to­ry’s Secret Heroes pod­cast from the BBC above, only long after his death in 1975 did his daugh­ter Simone prop­er­ly dis­cov­er and appre­ci­ate the con­tents of those vol­umes that had always sat on her father’s shelf. The con­fus­ing, even fright­en­ing cut-and-paste imagery and the poems she could only under­stand after learn­ing Ger­man turned out to con­tain unre­lent­ing attacks on the Third Reich and its lead­ers, the kind of mate­r­i­al that could have led to sum­ma­ry exe­cu­tion if dis­cov­ered. One issue even con­tained a poem Bloch wrote for his moth­er and sis­ter, not know­ing that they’d already died in the camps.

Now you can read all 96 issues of Het Onder­wa­ter-Cabaret online at Curt-Bloch.com, where they’ve been not just dig­i­tized but anno­tat­ed with intro­duc­tions and trans­la­tions of the orig­i­nal Ger­man and Dutch texts. There are also record­ed per­for­mances by actors, cabaret artists, and even oth­er Holo­caust sur­vivors. It makes Bloch’s clan­des­tine pro­duc­tiv­i­ty all the more impres­sive to remem­ber that zine cul­ture as we know it did­n’t exist at that time, let alone the instan­ta­neous glob­al dis­tri­b­u­tion net­work on which you’re read­ing this post right now. No mat­ter how tiny his read­er­ship, how mea­ger his resources, or how dire the pun­ish­ment for dar­ing to write crit­i­cal­ly about the regime, he sim­ply had to cre­ate, and he had to do it with a sense of humor. When com­ing up against frus­tra­tions in our own work, we’d do well to imag­ine Bloch run­ning his one-man cabaret out of the attic, scis­sors and glue in hand, and ask our­selves what our excuse is.

entries.title: Martin Scorsese Creates a List of 39 Essential Foreign Films for a Young Filmmaker
entries.summary: As a young man, filmmaker Colin Levy got an opportunity of a lifetime. He got a one-on-one meeting with Martin Scorsese. After spending much of his time in high school making a five-minute short, Levy won the national YoungArts award — and, with it, the chance to chat with the guy who directed Goodfellas, Taxi […]
entries.content:
As a young man, film­mak­er Col­in Levy got an oppor­tu­ni­ty of a life­time. He got a one-on-one meet­ing with Mar­tin Scors­ese. After spend­ing much of his time in high school mak­ing a five-minute short, Levy won the nation­al Youn­gArts award — and, with it, the chance to chat with the guy who direct­ed Good­fel­las, Taxi Dri­ver and Rag­ing Bull.

After get­ting a per­son­al tour of Scorsese’s office and edit­ing bays by none oth­er than leg­endary edi­tor Thel­ma Schoon­mak­er, Levy met the man him­self. “It was a defin­ing moment in my path as a film­mak­er,” he lat­er wrote on his blog.

Mar­tin Scors­ese was intim­i­dat­ing, to say the least. But very jovial, very talk­a­tive, and he took me seri­ous­ly. (Or con­vinced me, at least.) I pret­ty much kept my mouth shut. Every 30 sec­onds he would men­tion an actor, pro­duc­er, direc­tor or film title I had nev­er heard of before. I was stunned just to be in his pres­ence. He liked my film, he said. “How did you do the lit­tle crea­tures?” I tried to explain how I fig­ured out the basics of 3D ani­ma­tion. His eyes lit up and he start­ed talk­ing about the dig­i­tal effects in The Avi­a­tor.

The jux­ta­po­si­tion of scales was over­pow­er­ing. I felt like I was in a movie. Why he spent so much time with me I do not know, but it was amaz­ing just to be in his pres­ence. A few weeks after­wards I labored over a thank-you card, in which I expressed the over­whelm­ing impres­sion I had got­ten that I don’t know enough about any­thing. I spe­cial­ly don’t know enough about film his­to­ry and for­eign cin­e­ma. I asked if he had any sug­ges­tions for where to start.

A cou­ple of weeks lat­er, Scorsese’s assis­tant sent him a hand­ful of books and 39 for­eign movies per­son­al­ly picked by the film­mak­er. “Mr. Scors­ese asked that I send this your way,” his assis­tant wrote to Col­in. “This should be a jump start to your film edu­ca­tion!”

Scorsese’s selec­tions – which you can see above – are a fas­ci­nat­ing insight into what influ­enced the film­mak­er. Sev­er­al movies are peren­ni­al film school clas­sics: Ital­ian neo­re­al­ist mas­ter­pieces like The Bicy­cle Thief and Umber­to D pop up on the list along with ground­break­ing French New Wave works like The 400 Blows and Breath­less. More unex­pect­ed are sur­pris­ing­ly strong show­ings of both Japan­ese post-war movies and New Ger­man cin­e­ma. Both Aki­ra Kuro­sawa and Rain­er Wern­er Fass­binder get three films each. And while there are some rather eccen­tric, unex­pect­ed inclu­sions in the list–Roc­co and His Broth­ers? Il Sor­pas­so? Death by Hang­ing? – there are also some pret­ty strik­ing omis­sions; big name art house fig­ures like Ing­mar Bergman, Robert Bres­son and most sur­pris­ing­ly Fed­eri­co Felli­ni didn’t make the cut. In any case, as Scorsese’s assis­tant writes, this list is a great place to start for any­one look­ing to learn more about for­eign film.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2014.

Relat­ed Con­tent:

entries.title: If Fritz Lang’s Iconic Film Metropolis Had a Kraftwerk Soundtrack
entries.summary: The case of the copyright history of Fritz Lang’s influential sci-fi masterpiece Metropolis is as convoluted as the history of its film print. Lang’s vision and his original almost-three-hour cut were doomed to censorship right from the start. The Nazis took out its more socialist scenes. It’s been edited, colorized, put back together and restored. […]
entries.content:
The case of the copy­right his­to­ry of Fritz Lang’s influ­en­tial sci-fi mas­ter­piece Metrop­o­lis is as con­vo­lut­ed as the his­to­ry of its film print. Lang’s vision and his orig­i­nal almost-three-hour cut were doomed to cen­sor­ship right from the start. The Nazis took out its more social­ist scenes. It’s been edit­ed, col­orized, put back togeth­er and restored. Wikipedia cur­rent­ly lists nine dif­fer­ent ver­sions. Sim­i­lar­ly, own­er­ship of the film shift­ed from dis­trib­u­tors back to the pub­lic domain, then out of it again, once more of the orig­i­nal footage was redis­cov­ered. And then came 2023, when Metrop­o­lis once again land­ed in the pub­lic domain, at least in Amer­i­ca. Will we see as many legal bat­tles as new remix­es and re-scores? Prob­a­bly a bit of both.

The film’s orig­i­nal orches­tral score is avail­able, but many fans also seek out a score more befit­ting its futur­ist ori­gins. Some­thing more elec­tron­ic.

In fact, the four-minute clip above is YouTu­ber “Kar­maGer­many’s” 2009 fan-made edit using the music of Kraftwerk. If any band of the late 20th cen­tu­ry was born to be paired with Lang’s tech­no­log­i­cal vision, it’s the Fab Four from Düs­sel­dorf. Their icy roman­tic melodies strike the right bal­ance between Metrop­o­lis’ bat­tle, then syn­the­sis, of machin­ery and the human heart. And, look Kraftwerk even cre­at­ed a song called “Metrop­o­lis,” which becomes the actu­al score above. 

Like watch­ing the Wiz­ard of Oz while Dark Side of the Moon plays, Kraftwerk’s “Metrop­o­lis” seems writ­ten for the film, with its open­ing fan­fare over the shots of the future city wak­ing up, then how it switch­es to its motorik beat as the work­ers begin their alien­at­ing fac­to­ry day. (We haven’t done a side-by-side of the extant cut of the film, so there very well may be some edit­ing at play here.)

Now, while this is just a fan’s very well made use of the band’s full cat­a­log (it dives back into the band’s spaci­er ear­ly work for the film’s more ten­der moment), oth­ers have gone a more offi­cial route. Kraftwerk con­tem­po­rary and mem­ber of Clus­ter, Dieter Moe­bius record­ed a four-part, 40-minute suite Musik für Metrop­o­lis. It was released posthu­mous­ly in 2015, and it is one of his spook­i­er works.

Pri­or to that, tech­no DJ and com­pos­er Jeff Mills (no rela­tion) com­posed an hour-long score in 2000 that also had its own accom­pa­ny­ing edit, and mar­ried his career in both ambi­ent and futur­is­tic elec­tron­ic beats.

If the Kraftwerk re-edit whets your tech­no whis­tle, that clip was just the open­ing scene of the 90-minute fan edit from John McWilliam. His notes: “Orig­i­nal­ly two and a half hours long it has been reduced down to one hour 23 min­utes to pace it up includ­ing remov­ing the sub­ti­tle cards between shots and plac­ing them over [the] pic­ture instead.”

The last instruc­tion from McWilliam could apply to what­ev­er score you choose, as long as it’s for Metrop­o­lis: “Best watched on a big-ass TV hooked up to a big-booty sound sys­tem.”

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2022.

entries.title: A New Search Engine Lets You Explore 4 Million Works of Art & Historical Photographs from Museums and Libraries Around the World
entries.summary: We live in an age when you can describe practically anything you want to see in words, then see it almost immediately. Nobody will ever have laid eyes upon that particular sight before — and quite possibly, nobody ever will again. There we have both the upside and the downside of artificial intelligence-powered image generation. […]
entries.content:
We live in an age when you can describe prac­ti­cal­ly any­thing you want to see in words, then see it almost imme­di­ate­ly. Nobody will ever have laid eyes upon that par­tic­u­lar sight before — and quite pos­si­bly, nobody ever will again. There we have both the upside and the down­side of arti­fi­cial intel­li­gence-pow­ered image gen­er­a­tion. A con­stant flow of visu­al, aur­al, or tex­tu­al nov­el­ty offers stim­u­la­tion, to put it mild­ly, but it inevitably comes to feel insub­stan­tial. How­ev­er com­plex­ly derived from the work of human­i­ty it may be, it lacks a direct con­nec­tion to that work. Not so the results deliv­ered by Arkivism, a new search engine that responds to descrip­tions by draw­ing on a col­lec­tion of more than four mil­lion pieces of real art and pho­tog­ra­phy.

You may need a “town at sun­set,” a “col­or­ful cake,” a “rock­et ship blast­ing off,” a “Japan­ese wood­block print of a cat,” or some­thing else besides. Arkivism will more than like­ly be able to come up with more than a few images to fit the bill, with sources at hand includ­ing the Library of Con­gress, the NASA Video and Image Library, the Rijksmu­se­um, and Japan’s Nation­al Diet Library. (I notice that its reach extends even to the Gongu Copy­right Com­mis­sion in Korea, where I live, which will make it my go-to site when next I need to evoke the Joseon Dynasty.) The chance of dis­cov­er­ing a work of art you’d nev­er heard of is always high, even if you search a big name like Rem­brandt, Leonar­do, Klimt, or Hoku­sai.

“Every work indexed here is CC0 or pub­lic domain,” says Arkivis­m’s about page. “Down­load it, adapt it, use it in client work — no per­mis­sion need­ed, no strings.” Like all the best online ser­vices, this one was designed to answer the actu­al needs of its cre­ator, “a design­er and video cre­ator who kept need­ing imagery that was gen­uine­ly safe to use — and kept los­ing after­noons to a dozen muse­um search box­es.” Even if your work has noth­ing to do with design or video cre­ation, you nev­er know when you’ll be look­ing for a pic­ture of a cas­tle, a paint­ing of a feast, or a map of the world. Sure, you could always ask AI to gen­er­ate one for you, and you’d get some­thing more or less usable. Some­times that’s what you need; oth­er times, you’re ready to be led down a his­tor­i­cal and cul­tur­al rab­bit hole. Enter Arkivism here.

via Kot­tke

entries.title: The San Francisco Public Library Launches a Free Online Archive with 80,000+ Historical Images & Documents to Explore & Download
entries.summary: Over 100,000 people move to the San Francisco Bay Area each year. Their motivations for doing so no doubt vary, but these days, the ambition to make a fortune at the epicenter of the tech industry — especially amid the rapidly inflating AI bubble — is hardly unheard of. Unfortunately, that desire can be so […]
entries.content:
Over 100,000 peo­ple move to the San Fran­cis­co Bay Area each year. Their moti­va­tions for doing so no doubt vary, but these days, the ambi­tion to make a for­tune at the epi­cen­ter of the tech indus­try — espe­cial­ly amid the rapid­ly inflat­ing AI bub­ble — is hard­ly unheard of. Unfor­tu­nate­ly, that desire can be so all-con­sum­ing as to crowd out any inter­est in, or even curios­i­ty about, the city itself, to say noth­ing of its wider region. Yet the San Fran­cis­co we know today is the result of a sto­ry at least 250 years long, very lit­tle of which has much to do with ven­ture cap­i­tal or GPUs. Now, any­one who does want to make a start on under­stand­ing it can do so at the new-and-improved plat­form Dig­i­talSF, with its more than 80,000 his­tor­i­cal items avail­able to view and down­load.

An oper­a­tion of the San Fran­cis­co Pub­lic Library, Dig­i­talSF offers simul­ta­ne­ous access to mul­ti­ple online his­tor­i­cal archives. Search for the Gold­en Gate Bridge, let’s say, and the results will include hun­dreds of post­card pho­tographs and oth­er images cap­tur­ing that icon­ic piece of infra­struc­ture from a vari­ety of angles and in a vari­ety of decades, as well as — since this is the always cli­mat­i­cal­ly sur­pris­ing San Fran­cis­co we’re talk­ing about — under a vari­ety of weath­er con­di­tions.

The same exer­cise would prove equal­ly illu­mi­nat­ing for Chi­na­town, Pier 39, the Sutro Baths (which weren’t always ruins), and the Fer­ry Build­ing (which was­n’t always a col­lec­tion of pricey shops). Inevitably, this sort of vir­tu­al tourism becomes a form of time trav­el.

Dig­i­talSF also offers count­less glimpses of San Fran­cis­co’s impor­tant peri­ods in twen­ti­eth-cen­tu­ry Amer­i­can coun­ter­cul­ture, when the city made every­thing seem pos­si­ble: beat­nik poet­ry, the Grate­ful Dead, a par­tic­u­lar fla­vor of punk, the ascent of Har­vey Milk. But even before then, San Fran­cis­co had already expe­ri­enced a dis­pro­por­tion­ate­ly intense amount of his­to­ry dur­ing its rel­a­tive­ly short exis­tence: the earth­quakes of 1868 and 1906, for exam­ple, or the Gold Rush of the late eigh­teen-for­ties from whose par­tic­i­pants the local foot­ball team took its name. Those “forty-nin­ers” who flood­ed in from all over the rest of the Unit­ed States, turn­ing San Fran­cis­co from a small port town into a rel­a­tive­ly major city prac­ti­cal­ly overnight, prob­a­bly had scant fas­ci­na­tion with local his­to­ry them­selves. After all, they were too busy mak­ing it. Enter the Dig­i­talSF here.

entries.title: Soviet Animations of Winnie the Pooh, Created by the Innovative Animator Fyodor Khitruk
entries.summary: In 1962, the animator Fyodor Khitruk made his directorial debut with Story of One Crime, a film that broke with a Soviet tendency to make imitations of Disney-style animations. The film, as The Guardian explained in its 2012 obituary for the animator, came as a shock. It was stylistically simple and dealt with themes that Disney films would never […]
entries.content:
In 1962, the ani­ma­tor Fyo­dor Khitruk made his direc­to­r­i­al debut with Sto­ry of One Crime, a film that broke with a Sovi­et ten­den­cy to make imi­ta­tions of Dis­ney-style ani­ma­tions. The film, as The Guardian explained in its 2012 obit­u­ary for the ani­ma­tor, came as a shock. It was styl­is­ti­cal­ly sim­ple and dealt with themes that Dis­ney films would nev­er touch — like, why would a polite clerk mur­der two house­wives with a fry­ing pan?

Khitruk made oth­er films that were packed with social com­men­tary, often tak­ing aim at abus­es in the Sovi­et sys­tem. But, he also made straight­for­ward ani­ma­tions for chil­dren, none more famous than his series of films based on AA Mil­ne’s beloved Win­nie the Pooh books.

Cre­at­ed between 1969 and 1972, Khitruk’s three films star a bear named “Vin­ni-Pukh” who looks noth­ing like the Win­nie the Pooh that West­ern­ers grew up with. (You can see the orig­i­nal illus­tra­tions of Pooh by E.H. Shep­ard here.) But view­ers will cer­tain­ly rec­og­nize the sto­ry­line and spir­it of the orig­i­nal Pooh in the Sovi­et adap­ta­tions. For decades, these films have enchant­ed East Euro­pean view­ers, both young and old. And they still occa­sion­al­ly appear on Russ­ian TV.

Above, you can watch the three ani­ma­tions online. They appear in the order in which they were released: 1) Win­nie-the-Pooh (Винни-Пух, 1969), 2) Win­nie-the-Pooh Goes on a Vis­it (Винни-Пух идет в гости, 1971); and 3) Win­nie-the-Pooh and the Day of Con­cern (Винни-Пух и день забот, 1972).

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2013.

entries.title: A Beginner’s Guide to Philosophy: From Logic to Epistemology to Metaphysics
entries.summary: These are, perhaps, not the very best times for humanities majors. Seldom do we even hear the once-standard defense that, by pursuing a course of study in subjects of that kind, students “learn how to think.” Such a justification still points to real value, at least in the most demanding settings. entries.content:
These are, per­haps, not the very best times for human­i­ties majors. Sel­dom do we even hear the once-stan­dard defense that, by pur­su­ing a course of study in sub­jects of that kind, stu­dents “learn how to think.” Such a jus­ti­fi­ca­tion still points to real val­ue, at least in the most demand­ing set­tings. Take Har­vard’s course Human­i­ties 10, whose dig­i­tal device-free envi­ron­ment and syl­labus cov­er­ing every­thing from The Odyssey and Ulysses to Pla­to and James Bald­win — at a pace of one sub­stan­tial book per week — recent­ly drew the atten­tion of the Wall Street Jour­nal. Yet it’s always been true that you don’t have to major in any­thing to learn how to think, or in any case, to make a start of doing so.

Take the phi­los­o­phy-and-lit­er­a­ture YouTu­ber Jared Hen­der­son, who in the video at the top of the post tells us how he began his self-direct­ed study in high school. “I did what a lot of peo­ple would think is nat­ur­al,” he says. “I went to a book­store, and then I just found some books that I want­ed to read.” The pieces of light read­ing he took home: Friedrich Niet­zsche’s The Birth of Tragedy and Mar­tin Hei­deg­ger’s Intro­duc­tion to Meta­physics.

“If you know any­thing about phi­los­o­phy, I think you know that that was prob­a­bly not the ide­al way to start.” But all the years of learn­ing and teach­ing since have final­ly put him in a posi­tion of know­ing how to begin, and in the span of half an hour, he lays out an intel­lec­tu­al roadmap for any­one in the same posi­tion as his teenage self, with stops in log­ic, meta­physics, epis­te­mol­o­gy, ethics, and polit­i­cal phi­los­o­phy.

That sequence reflects the rea­son­able assump­tion that, before we can eval­u­ate argu­ments about how soci­ety ought to be arranged, we must learn to eval­u­ate state­ments about how things are. We must, in oth­er words, learn how to think — but also learn about the nature of real­i­ty itself, and how or whether we can know any­thing about it in the first place, ques­tions rel­e­vant to both meta­physics and epis­te­mol­o­gy. That may seem like a daunt­ing task, but Hen­der­son frames all its stages in rela­tion to one anoth­er, nam­ing some of the most famous philoso­phers who have writ­ten in the rel­e­vant fields along the way. No sin­gle read­ing could give you mas­tery of their work, or even a full under­stand­ing of it, how­ev­er clear the big­ger pic­ture might seem. But the attempt teach­es the true first les­son of phi­los­o­phy: in one area of knowl­edge or anoth­er, you’ll always be a begin­ner.

entries.title: Watch David Bowie Take MTV to Task for Failing to Play Music Videos by Black Artists (1983)
entries.summary: The old vaudeville phrase “Will it play in Peoria?” has its roots in the late 19th century, specifically in Horatio Alger’s novel Five Hundred Dollars; Or Jacob Marlowe’s Secret. Like all of the books Alger wrote extolling the virtues of thrift, study, grooming, industry, etc., this one articulates a middle American bootstraps philosophy and rags-to-riches mythology, while […]
entries.content:
The old vaude­ville phrase “Will it play in Peo­ria?” has its roots in the late 19th cen­tu­ry, specif­i­cal­ly in Hor­a­tio Alger’s nov­el Five Hun­dred Dol­lars; Or Jacob Marlowe’s Secret. Like all of the books Alger wrote extolling the virtues of thrift, study, groom­ing, indus­try, etc., this one artic­u­lates a mid­dle Amer­i­can boot­straps phi­los­o­phy and rags-to-rich­es mythol­o­gy, while giv­ing the enter­tain­ment indus­try a col­or­ful way to sum up the small-town audi­ences who embraced Alger’s strait-laced eth­ic, and who need­ed to be pan­dered to or they wouldn’t get all those big-city jokes and ref­er­ences.

Peo­ria has been many places in the U.S.—from Tul­sa to Boise—but what­ev­er the test mar­ket, the assump­tions have always been the same: the Amer­i­can main­stream is insu­lar, mid­dle class or aspir­ing to it, cul­tur­al­ly con­ser­v­a­tive, unfail­ing­ly white, and fear­ful of every­one who isn’t. Such demo­graph­ic dog­ma has per­sist­ed for over a hun­dred years. Even when it is shown to be out­mod­ed or plain wrong, broad­cast­ers and jour­nal­ists con­tin­ue to play to Peo­ria, gen­u­flect­ing to a sta­t­ic, pop­ulist ver­sion of the U.S. that ignores large, rapid­ly chang­ing seg­ments of the pop­u­la­tion.

In the ear­ly eight­ies it took an Eng­lish­man with a very high pro­file to inter­ro­gate this state of affairs on the air. You may have come across the inter­view after David Bowie died, when social media filled with trib­utes and remem­brances. One thread that got a lot of atten­tion involved the tran­script of a 1983 inter­view Bowie gave the fledg­ling MTV, in which he “turns the tables on reporter Mark Good­man,” writes Takepart’s Jen­nifer Swann, “to grill him about the youth-ori­ent­ed network’s lack of eth­nic diver­si­ty.”

“It’s a sol­id enter­prise, and it’s got a lot going for it,” says Bowie. “I’m just floored by the fact there’s so few black artists fea­tured in it. Why is that?” On the spot, Good­man reach­es for a mar­ket­ing term, “nar­row­cast­ing,” to sug­gest that the net­work is delib­er­ate­ly tar­get­ing a niche. But when Bowie keeps push­ing, Good­man admits that the “nar­row” demo­graph­ic is the very same sup­posed mass mar­ket that exist­ed in Alger’s day, when the only rep­re­sen­ta­tions of black enter­tain­ers most white audi­ences in Peo­ria (or wher­ev­er) saw were in black­face.

We have to try and do what we think not only New York and Los Ange­les will appre­ci­ate, but also Pough­keep­sie or the Mid­west. Pick some town in the Mid­west that would be scared to death by Prince, which we’re play­ing, or a string of oth­er black faces, or black music. We have to play music we think an entire coun­try is going to like, and cer­tain­ly we’re a rock and roll sta­tion.

What do the Isley Broth­ers, asks Good­man, mean to a sev­en­teen-year-old? To which Bowie replies, “I’ll tell you what the Isley Broth­ers mean to a black sev­en­teen-year-old, and sure­ly he’s part of Amer­i­ca as well.” To the defense that it’s just the way things are, espe­cial­ly in radio, he gives a reply that might be derid­ed by many in the ready-made terms that rou­tine­ly pop up in such dis­cus­sions these days. Bowie, who suc­cess­ful­ly crossed over into play­ing for black audi­ences on Soul Train in the mid-sev­en­ties, would have sneered at phras­es like “SJW.” As he says in response to one young fan who rant­ed in a let­ter about “what he did­n’t want to see” on MTV: “Well that’s his prob­lem.”

The Peo­ria effect, says Bowie, “does seem to be ram­pant through Amer­i­can media. Should it not be a chal­lenge to make the media far more inte­grat­ed, espe­cial­ly, if any­thing, in musi­cal terms?” The “lines are begin­ning to blur,” Good­man admits. At the end of that year, Michael Jackson’s John Lan­dis-direct­ed “Thriller” video debuted and “changed music videos for­ev­er,” break­ing the prime­time bar­ri­ers for black artists on MTV, trans­form­ing the net­work “into a cul­tur­al behe­moth,” as Swann writes, and giv­ing the lie to the Peo­ria myth, one Bowie knew had lit­tle to do in actu­al­i­ty with the country’s cul­ture or its tastes but with a nar­row, archa­ic view of who the media should serve.

See Good­man’s full inter­view with Bowie just above.
